settings.editor:
Every summer has the same thermostat debate. One person wants the house at 68°F, another is watching the electric bill climb, and everyone is trying to stay comfortable through Louisiana heat and humidity.

Both sides have a point. Comfort matters, especially when the air outside feels heavy and sticky. But constantly lowering the thermostat is not always the answer. In many homes, it only makes the AC run longer, increases energy use, and puts more strain on the system without solving the real comfort problem.

The best approach is to choose thermostat settings your AC can maintain efficiently while still controlling humidity. Here is how to find the right balance for your home this summer.

The best thermostat settings for summer are usually around 78°F when you are home, 82°F to 85°F when you are away, and 74°F to 78°F while sleeping, depending on your comfort needs. But in Dry Prong, LA, and nearby Central Louisiana communities, the right setting is not just about the number on the screen. High humidity can make your home feel warmer, even when the thermostat looks reasonable. For the best balance of comfort and savings, pair smart thermostat settings with good airflow, clean filters, humidity control, and regular AC maintenance.

You may have heard that 78°F is the recommended summer thermostat setting when you are home. That can be a good starting point, but in Central Louisiana, comfort depends heavily on humidity.
A home set to 78°F may feel comfortable if the AC is removing moisture properly. But if humidity is high, that same 78°F can feel warm, sticky, and uncomfortable.

Your comfort depends on more than temperature, including:

  • Indoor humidity levels
  • Airflow from vents
  • Ceiling fan use
  • Insulation and sun exposure
  • Filter condition
  • AC system performance
  • Ductwork and air leaks

That is why the best thermostat setting is not always the lowest setting. It is the setting your system can maintain while keeping the air comfortable and balanced.

settings.title: Best Thermostat Setting When You Are Home

settings.editor:
For many households, 78°F is a smart starting point when you are home and awake. It can help limit unnecessary AC runtime while still keeping the house comfortable.

If 78°F feels too warm, do not immediately drop the thermostat to 70°F. Try adjusting one degree at a time and give your system time to respond.

You can also improve comfort without lowering the thermostat by:

  • Running ceiling fans counterclockwise
  • Closing blinds during peak sun hours
  • Replacing dirty air filters
  • Keeping vents open and clear
  • Reducing indoor heat from ovens or appliances
  • Scheduling AC maintenance if airflow feels weak

If your home still feels uncomfortable at 76°F to 78°F, the issue may not be the thermostat. Your AC may be struggling with airflow, humidity control, dirty coils, or system efficiency.

settings.title: Best Thermostat Setting When You Are Away

settings.editor:
When no one is home for several hours, raising the thermostat to 82°F to 85°F can help reduce cooling costs. This keeps the house from getting extremely hot while reducing unnecessary AC runtime.

In Louisiana, it is usually better to raise the thermostat instead of turning the AC off completely. If your home gets too hot and humid while you are away, your system may have to work harder later to cool the space and remove moisture.

A programmable or smart thermostat can help by automatically adjusting the temperature based on your schedule. For example, it can raise the temperature while you are at work, then start cooling before you return home.

This helps avoid two common problems: wasting energy cooling an empty house and coming home to a hot, uncomfortable space.

Sleep comfort is personal, but many homeowners prefer 74°F to 78°F at night. If you need a cooler bedroom, try comfort strategies before dropping the thermostat too low.

Helpful options include:

  • Using ceiling fans
  • Choosing breathable bedding
  • Closing curtains earlier in the day
  • Keeping bedroom doors open for better airflow
  • Checking whether the bedroom gets weaker airflow than other rooms

If one room is always hot at night, the thermostat setting may not be the real issue. You may have ductwork problems, poor insulation, blocked vents, or an AC system that needs service.

settings.title: Why Lowering The Thermostat Does Not Cool Your Home Faster

settings.editor:
This is one of the most common summer myths. Setting your thermostat to 65°F will not make most residential AC systems cool faster. It simply tells the system to keep running until it reaches that lower temperature.

That extra runtime can lead to:

  • Higher energy bills
  • More wear on the AC system
  • Longer cooling cycles
  • Greater risk of breakdown during peak heat
  • Poorer humidity control if the system is not operating properly

A better approach is to choose a realistic setting, improve airflow, control heat gain, and make sure your system is maintained. Energy.gov also advises homeowners to avoid setting the thermostat colder than normal when first turning on the AC, since it will not cool the home faster and may increase energy costs.

settings.title: Should You Turn The AC Off When You Leave?

settings.editor:
For most homes in Dry Prong and Central Louisiana, turning the AC off completely during summer is usually not the best strategy. Indoor temperatures can rise quickly, and humidity can build inside the home.

That can make your house feel uncomfortable when you return and may force your system to run for a long time to recover.

Instead, raise the thermostat by several degrees while you are away. This gives your AC a break without letting heat and humidity take over. According to Energy.gov’s guidance on programmable thermostats, setting your thermostat back 7°F to 10°F for 8 hours a day can help save as much as 10% a year on heating and cooling.

settings.title: Smart Thermostats Help, But They Cannot Fix Everything

settings.editor:
A smart thermostat can make it easier to control cooling costs. It can follow your schedule, adjust temperatures automatically, and help prevent waste when no one is home. ENERGY STAR explains that certified smart thermostats are independently verified based on field data to deliver energy savings.

But it cannot fix every comfort issue.

A smart thermostat will not solve:

  • Dirty filters
  • Weak airflow
  • Leaky ducts
  • Poor insulation
  • Refrigerant issues
  • Dirty coils
  • An aging or undersized AC system

If your AC runs constantly, blows warm air, or cannot keep up with normal thermostat settings, it may be time to schedule AC repair.

settings.title: Get Better Comfort From Your Summer Thermostat Settings

settings.editor:
The best thermostat settings for summer are a useful starting point, but real comfort depends on more than temperature. In Dry Prong and Central Louisiana, humidity, airflow, insulation, and AC performance all affect how your home feels.

Start with 78°F when home, 82°F to 85°F when away, and 74°F to 78°F while sleeping. Then adjust based on your comfort, energy bills, and how well your system maintains indoor humidity.

If your home still feels warm, humid, or unevenly cooled despite reasonable thermostat settings, the thermostat may not be the real problem.
